data.title: Tracking U.S., state and county gas prices, in maps and charts
data.description: The war in Iran has led to higher prices at the gas pump. Gas prices in the United States, up by more than 40% since the U.S. and Israel launched the war, have soared as the global oil supply constricts. Now at a national average of more than $4 per gallon, according to data from motor club AAA, this price increase is straining already-stretched budgets in households across the country. NBC News is tracking gas prices and how they change at the national, state and county levels, and will be updating this article daily with the latest data. Average gas prices have increased more than a dollar since the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran. In six states — Alaska, California, Hawaii, Oregon, Nevada and Washington — average gas prices are at least $5 per gallon. Georgia, Ohio and Texas are paying the least, according to AAA data. According to a Brown University analysis, the increase in gas prices since the start of the war has cost Americans more than $70 billion. Fuel costs aren’t limited to gas. Jet fuel prices have been surging as well, leading airlines to increase airfares. Oil prices have spiked, then see-sawed, were approaching pre-war levels, and are now surging again as turmoil in the Middle East continues. Since mid-May, the average national gas price has declined by around 20 cents. The average price is still up more than a dollar per gallon since the start of the war.

data.title: Americans’ eating habits are changing. For Chick-fil-A, adapting to them is a tall order
data.description: Chick-fil-A is a company that cherishes its past. The third-largest restaurant chain in America hasn’t changed the recipe for its signature chicken sandwich since it debuted in 1967. From the beginning, Chick-fil-A has been a private, family-owned business and it intends to stay that way.

data.title: Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living increase in 2027
data.description: Social Security recipients will receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment next year of 3.6%, one of the largest increases this decade. But advocates say it’s still unlikely to go far enough for many struggling seniors. The increase is the largest since 2022, and will amount to an average monthly increase of about $70, according to the Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group for older Americans. Elevated inflation continues to bedevil the U.S. economy, with rising energy and gas prices sparked by wars in Iran and Ukraine as the primary culprits. Yet even without the added cost of gas, so-called core inflation — which excludes volatile energy and food prices — has remained stuck at about 2.5%, well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target. For senior citizens, who are the majority of Social Security retirement benefit recipients, next year’s increase will be welcome, but it will still come up short given rising costs, said Shannon Benton, the league’s executive director. “Seniors have spent years watching their expenses outpacing their benefits,” Benton said. “This provides a little breathing room but won’t undo the damage of what we’ve seen this decade.” The league found in a survey that 89% of older Americans thought the cost-of-living adjustment that kicked in this year, 2.8%, was inadequate given rising costs in the economy. About 44% of seniors draw all their income from Social Security, the survey found. The annual adjustment is typically calculated using inflation data from July, August and September. But it uses an obscure inflation index that advocates say doesn’t accurately reflect seniors’ spending priorities, which include more medical and prescription drug costs, as well as a greater likelihood that they will pay rent and generally higher home energy costs. Those categories have historically outpaced headline inflation, though the rate of medical-cost increases has slowed recently. One reform proposal would index the annual adjustment to more precisely reflect seniors’ needs — but Benton said it is unlikely to be adopted until all of Social Security is overhauled. “They need Social Security benefits to cover the cost of living, and it’s just not happening,” she said.

data.title: How grocery prices have changed since Trump took office
data.description: Are President Donald Trump’s policies bringing down grocery bills? Grocery prices have been on the rise for most of the past six years, as the war in Iran, supply chain bottlenecks, the war in Ukraine and excessive profit-taking here in the U.S. have put a strain on consumers’ wallets. Trump campaigned heavily on the price of food in 2024, promising that if elected he would lower costs. Has that happened? To find out, NBC News is tracking the average grocery price of eggs, ground beef, and other common grocery-basket goods. The average price of eggs — a frequent stand-in for inflation during the campaign — have declined from a spring 2025 peak and are now down 31% since Trump took office last year. Average orange juice prices are up 23% and ground beef prices are up 17% from January 2025. Since 2021, NBC News has monitored the average point-of-sale price for eggs, chicken, bread, ground beef and other common grocery items. The graphic below shows their current average prices, along with how much those prices have changed since Trump took office in 2025. The grocery price data, provided by the global marketing research firm NIQ, is collected from real checkout prices paid nationwide at grocery stores, drugstores, mass merchandisers, selected dollar stores, selected warehouse clubs and military commissaries. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ monthly consumer price index, which uses human data collectors and includes other food product categories, is another resource for average price data. This article will be updated twice each month.

data.title: Starbucks is ‘not buying Chipotle’ after reports it had explored a deal
data.description: Starbucks on Monday said that it would not be moving to buy Chipotle Mexican Grill, after a report last week said the coffee house chain had evaluated the prospect. “As a matter of policy, we don’t comment on rumors and speculation, but we want to be clear we are not buying Chipotle,” a Starbucks spokesperson told NBC News in an emailed statement. “Our team is laser focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy,” they said, while adding that the company looked forward to sharing its latest financial results later in October. The announcement from Starbucks came after the Financial Times on Thursday reported that “Starbucks has explored a takeover of Chipotle Mexican Grill.” The report also stated that it had hired advisers to work on a takeover proposal for Chipotle. Starbucks responded to the report later Thursday by issuing a statement that did not definitively address the status of its interest in Chipotle. A deal between Starbucks and Chipotle would have been transformative for the restaurant and fast-casual dining sector. It would have also reunited Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol with Chipotle, the company he led until late 2024. In the immediate aftermath of the FT report, Starbucks shares fell, while Chipotle’s stock surged sharply higher. But over the last year, the two companies have been on different trajectories. Starbucks is in the midst of a vast turnaround program, which Niccol has touted in recent weeks as delivering progress. Over the last year, Starbucks shares have risen 15%. On the other hand, Chipotle’s shares have plunged 20% over the last 12 months. Both companies are grappling with broadly higher prices for consumers, lagging traffic and are trying to revive sales. Chipotle Mexican Grill did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.

data.title: To counteract a spooky economy, America prepares to spend on Halloween candy
data.description: This Halloween, the fright isn’t just at the haunted house. Rising prices for everything from groceries to gas are driving many consumers to cut back. “I’m walking to save a little bit of money,” said Lakisha Reardon, a legal assistant. “I’m bringing in my own lunch.” Reardon said she has especially seen her electric bill spike this year. She said she is paying an extra $150 every month. “I’m ready to invest in candles,” she said. But one thing she won’t give up? Halloween candy. Average prices for chewing gum and candy have soared 8.1% over the last year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Despite the higher prices, Americans are still buying treats. “I remember being a little kid and being super excited when I would get Reese’s Cups,” said Abby Mynatt, a college student who lives in Knoxville, Tennessee. “I want to give that to some other children.” Mynatt, 21, said she usually spends around $50 for Halloween candy. She is expecting to shell out a bit more money this year despite financial pressures. “I certainly think there are a little more tense things with my budget right now,” she said. “But I still think that certain things, even just little pleasures, are still worth it.” The price of non-chocolate candy items has averaged $3.31 this year, up 1.8% from last year, according to PwC. But Halloween chocolate prices have jumped 15.5%, to an average of $5.67 per package. Industry experts attribute the rise in chocolate prices partly to a cocoa shock over the last couple years. Extreme weather in key cocoa-producing countries like Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana sent global cocoa prices soaring — they quadrupled from January 2023 to January 2025, according to data from the International Monetary Fund. “Because chocolate makers buy cocoa months, sometimes up to two years ahead, shoppers are paying for that spike now,” said Ali Furman, PwC’s Consumer Markets Industry leader. “Cocoa prices have since fallen by about half, but lower costs take time to reach the shelf and won’t show up on shelves this Halloween season.” The market research firm NIQ has seen a more muted increase in prices, with chocolate overall up 9.4% from a year ago but Halloween-specific chocolate just up 1.7%. Analysts say tariffs this year aren’t helping, either. In July, the U.S. imposed tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on 60 trade partners. “Chocolate comes from elsewhere, so tariffs being added onto it have certainly increased costs that manufacturers are feeling as well,” said Chris Costagli, the leader of food and non-alcoholic beverage insights at NIQ. Still, the National Retail Federation projects that Halloween spending will soar to $13.5 billion this season, with 96% of Halloween shoppers expecting to buy sweets. It’s part of a broader trend this year of consumers leaning into little luxuries like makeup and movie tickets as an antidote for economic gloom. A lot of that gloom stems from concerns about inflation and the rising cost of living. Consumer prices have jumped 3.4% over the last year in large part due to rising energy costs, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. With wages up just 3% over the same period, paychecks aren’t keeping up with prices. It has led many people to forgo bigger purchases and cut back in small ways every day. Leonard Smith is planning to buy Halloween candy this year, but says he may cut back. “I don’t want to spend that much money because I need money for other things besides candy,” said Smith, 36, who lives in Delaware. But he has a strategy to save: Smith buys candy after Halloween when many stores slash prices. Ari Monahan, a nanny who describes herself as “like a Disney adult, but for Halloween,” said she may get candy that’s a little less expensive, but she still wants to treat the kids in her New York City neighborhood. “I want to be the good house,” she said. “There’s not that many kids in my area, so I want to give them a little prize for coming.” Monahan, 30, also buys little treats for herself. “Dark chocolate, a lot of coffees, anything pumpkin spice,” she said. “If it makes me smile and I have a little money, I’ll pay for it because everything is so grim right now,” she added. “A pair of socks with dachshunds on it, I’m like, ‘You know what? I can do that. I could swing it today.’” Monahan says rising prices are taking a big bite out of her paycheck, and she worries she might never be able to buy a house. Home prices are near record highs, and mortgage rates have spiked over the course of the war with Iran — with the 30-year fixed topping 7.6% earlier this month, a nearly 3-year high. It’s a double whammy that is putting a key pillar of the American dream further out of reach for many people. And yet in an economy where the big things might seem far away, there are always little treats to get by. “I’ve been in a real ‘buy yourself little treats’ mentality,” said Monahan. “I keep buying too much stuff for my dog. I guess I didn’t buy another dog. That’s saving, right?”

data.title: Gas cost calculator: How much have higher gas prices cost you?
data.description: After more than six months of war, does your wallet feel lighter? Since the Iran war started, Americans have spent an additional $70 billion on gasoline, according to a Brown University estimate. Increased gas prices have resulted in higher monthly expenses for individuals — anywhere from less than $20 to more than $300 for a driver who fills up twice a month, according to an NBC News analysis of motor club AAA’s average national gas price data. Just how much has the spike in gas prices bitten into your budget? Use our calculator to estimate your additional expenses at the pump since the start of the war. The calculator updates with the latest data daily. The cost model used in the calculator uses a sample of the average daily gas price in the United States since the start of the war, simulating how gas prices vary depending on which day you fuel up. The results you get will fall in a range of average costs and change slightly as you use the tool. Since Feb. 28, when the U.S. and Israel first struck Iran, average gas prices nationally have risen about 50%. U.S. gas prices in early May were among the most expensive those prices had been in the past decade at an average of $4.63 per gallon, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The average gas price last topped $4 in 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine. Faced with higher prices, some Americans are driving less, or at least filling up less often. An analysis by the location analytics company Placer.ai found gas station visits across the U.S. were down 5.7% the week of May 18, compared with the corresponding week in May 2025. At the state level, an NBC News analysis finds Utah residents are feeling the greatest strain since the start of the war, with gas prices up about 75% since February, averaging nearly $5.00 per gallon as of late September. Oklahoma and Wisconsin, in addition to Utah, have experienced the highest rates of change, with prices up about 70% from five months ago. Hawaii state’s gas prices have remained the most resilient, up less than 30% — about $1.10 — since February. To alleviate pain at the pump, some states have paused their gas taxes or postponed increases. Members of the Trump administration discussed pausing the federal gas tax, but they have yet to act on the initiative. Methodology This is how the NBC News gas cost calculator estimates the added costs: The calculator inputs the number of gallons in a refueling and the number of fill-ups per month, as provided by the reader, as well as average daily national gas prices from Feb. 28 to today.Based on the number of fill-ups, particular days’ per-gallon prices are sampled, reflecting how often a person may be going to the pump (every 10 days, 15 days, 30 days, etc.).The extra costs are calculated by subtracting the Feb. 28 per-gallon price from the average of the sampled prices. The result is then multiplied by the number of fill-ups and multiplied again by the number of gallons in the gas tank. Data is sourced from AAA’s daily posted national gas price averages and dates to Feb. 28. It updates with new daily numbers each morning.
